Kinetics of air mixing–anaerobic digestion: High organic substrate 
concentrations enhance system resistance to oxygen stress
Kailun Song a,b, Huan Chen a,b, Yue Zhao a,b, Li Chen a,b, Rong You a,b, Yilin Wang a,b,  
Hongnan Yang a,b, Wenguo Wang a,b, Liangwei Deng a,b,*
a Biogas Institute of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China
b Laboratory of Development and Application of Rural Renewable Energy, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu, 610041, PR China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Air mixing
Micro–oxygen
ORP
Methane
Models
A B S T R A C T
Air mixing–anaerobic digestion is proposed to overcome the limitations of traditional mixing methods, which can 
increase methane output and reduce H2S content. However, the effects of air mixing can be either inhibitory or 
facilitative, depending on the duration of oxygen stress and the elevated methane production rate. Kinetics 
models were developed to describe the variations (increase and decrease) in ORP and methane production. The 
results revealed that the increase in ORP was negatively correlated with the organic substrate concentration, but 
positively correlated with mixing intensity. The decrease in ORP showed a positive correlation with both the 
organic substrate concentration and the maximum ORP reached at the end of air mixing. The maximum rate of 
ORP increase and decrease were 66.0 mV/min and 3.03 mV/min, respectively. After air mixing stopped, when 
ORP decreased below −370 mV (0 mg/L DO), the methane production increased. The maximum methane 
production could be elevated to 358 mL/h at sufficient substrate. High organic substrate concentrations are 
critical for system resistance to oxygen-induced inhibition. This resistance is primarily achieved through 
accelerated oxygen consumption and stabilized anaerobic environments for methane production. The developed 
methane output models enable the quantitative prediction of methane output and offer guidance for optimizing 
air mixing parameters.
1. Introduction
The anaerobic digestion technology is an effective strategy for waste 
treatment and utilization, with the advantages of less energy con­
sumption, a high organic loading rate, and the ability to recover a clean 
energy source [1,2]. Proper mixing is the key to improving the efficiency 
of anaerobic digestion with high concentrations of suspended solids 
[3,4]. Mechanical mixing in the traditional method is characterized by 
high energy consumption, and difficult maintenance [5]. Biogas mixing 
has the advantages of simple maintenance and low equipment costs [6]. 
However, for biogas mixing, there are problems such as safety hazards 
and biogas shortages at start up phase [7]. To overcome these issues, our 
team proposed a novel strategy of using air to replace biogas as a carrier 
to drive mixing, and establish an innovative technology called air mix­
ing–anaerobic digestion [8,9]. Compared with mechanical mixing and 
biogas mixing, this technology was able to increase volumetric methane 
production by 6.4%–19.6%, and it also provides the added benefit of 
reducing H₂S in the biogas. Air mixing–anaerobic digestion has already 
been applied in full–scale biogas plants and has achieved superior per­
formance [10], primarily because air mixing not only improves the mass 
transfer efficiency between microorganisms and the substrate (with a 
relative contribution of 62.9%) but also creates a micro–oxygen envi­
ronment (with a relative contribution of 37.1%) [4,11]. Even though the 
micro–oxygen environment can effectively promote anaerobic diges­
tion, thereby resulting in increased methane production [12,13]. Inap­
propriate air mixing intensity and duration can lead to a decrease in the 
normal methane production time, thus leading to a reduction in the total 
methane output [10]. The effects of air mixing on the growth and 
metabolism of microorganisms and the performance of methane pro­
duction are clearly complex processes. To maintain efficient anaerobic 
digestion under air mixing condition, parameters such as intensity, time, 
and frequency must be precisely regulated. This requires the develop­
ment of kinetic models capable of optimizing these key mixing 
parameters.

Kinetic models have been widely used in studies of anaerobic 
digestion to describe biogas production, as well as to predict and regu­
late operational performance [14]. Kinetic models include mainly early 
experience models and process models. Many experience models have 
been developed such as the first–order kinetic model and the modified 
Gompertz model [15]. Process models that are based on biochemical 
reaction mechanisms include the Monod model [16], the Contois model 
[17], the Stovere Kincannon model [18], and the Chen–Hashimoto 
model [19,20] etc. In recent years, the kinetics of anaerobic digestion in 
a micro–oxygen environment have gradually attracted increasing 
attention [21]. The role of dissolved oxygen (DO) in various stages of 
anaerobic digestion was characterized by ADM1 [22]. However, only 
simple substrates such as glucose and primarily substrate degradation 
have been considered [23], and the effects of DO dynamics on methane 
production and ORP variation have been neglected. Moreover, the 
complexity of ADM1 limits its applicability in anaerobic digestion with 
complex substrates or actual plants. In particular, the ADM1-Ox (oxy­
gen) model incorporates 25 state variables and 22 biochemical pro­
cesses, making it difficult to obtain all required state variables in 
practical anaerobic digestion (biogas) plant [22]. Furthermore, due to 
the inherent complexity of anaerobic digestion systems, accurate mea­
surement of DO also presents considerable challenges.
Although air mixing–anaerobic digestion has been established, its 
optimization still relies on the development of appropriate kinetic 
models. To clarify the quantitative effects of air mixing on the ORP and 
methane production. Air mixing–anaerobic digestion experiments were 
carried out by using an anaerobic sequencing batch reactor (ASBR). 
Based on these experiments, kinetic models describing ORP variation 
(increase and decrease) and methane production were developed. 
Moreover, a integrated model for determining the mixing intensity, 
time, and frequency of air mixing–anaerobic digestion was established. 
These models developed in this study can lay the foundation for 
advancing air mixing–anaerobic digestion technology and challenge the 
conventional understanding of oxygen's role in anaerobic processes. 
Further investigation of oxygen-driven kinetics will not only fill the 
existing knowledge gap regarding the quantitative effects of oxygen on 
anaerobic digestion but also provide a theoretical basis for improving 
and optimizing this emerging air-mixing technology. Moreover, the 
findings also can offer new insights into methane emissions under micro- 
oxic and anaerobic conditions.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Laboratory–scale reactor, feedstock and inoculum
The reactor was an ASBR system with a diameter of 11 cm, length of 
45 cm, total volume of 4.5 L, and working volume of 4 L. It was equipped 
with an outer jacket, as well as an inlet and outlet for circulating heated 
water. Temperature was maintained at 35 ◦C by pumping hot water from 
a thermostatic bath through the jacket. Air for mixing was injected into 
the reactor via an air pump and an aeration tray at the bottom of the 
reactor. The reactor was equipped with pH, DO, and ORP probes con­
nected to a data recorder (M300, Mettler Toledo, Urdof, Switzerland).
The swine wastewater used as organic substrate of anaerobic diges­
tion was obtained from a farm in Jianyang City, Sichuan Province, 
China. A 0.85 mm (20 mesh) sieve was used to remove the large sus­
pended substance. The filtrate was stored at 4 ◦C. Before use, the filtrate 
was diluted with tap water to adjust the chemical oxygen demand (COD) 
concentration to the required level. The inoculum sludge was obtained 
from a mesophilic anaerobic digestion reactor treating swine manure. A 
detailed characterization of the swine wastewater and anaerobic inoc­
ulum sludge is shown in Table S1.
2.2. Experimental design
At the start of the experiment, 1.5 L of anaerobic inoculum sludge 
and 2.5 L of substrate were added to each of three identical reactors. The 
reactors were operated in an ASBR mode. Each daily cycle consisted of 
withdrawal, feeding, and reaction stages. At a fixed time each day, 1 L of 
digestate was first withdrawn and then fed with 1 L of swine wastewater 
prepared at the designated organic concentration. When the daily biogas 
production varied within 10% of the average value over a period of 1–2 
weeks, the reactor was considered to have reached steady state condi­
tions, and the experiment could be carried out.
2.2.1. Experimental design for the response of the ORP to DO variation in 
air mixing–anaerobic digestion
The swine wastewater used as organic substrate in the experiment 
was diluted so that the substrate concentration was 10 g COD/L. First, 
the organic substrate was added to the ASBR. After the ORP stabilized at 
approximately −450 to −460 mV, air mixing began at an intensity of 
66.7 mL air/min. The DO and ORP values were both recorded every 
minute with a data recorder. Mixing continued for 30 min, and data 
recording was stopped when the DO and ORP stabilized.
2.2.2. The effect of air mixing on ORP variation and methane production
After the ORP stabilized (at approximately −450 to −460 mV), the 
M300 recorder was started. The ORP values were recorded at 1 min 
intervals until the initial ORP recovered to the background values at the 
end. For each of the 5 organic substrate concentrations (2, 4, 6, 8, and 
10 g COD/L), air was pumped into the mixed liquid at flow rates (mixing 
intensities) of 0, 33.3, 66.7, and 100 mL air/min for 120 min. The biogas 
output and CH4 concentration were measured every 1 h for 24 h after the 
air mixing stopped. At the end of each experiment, the anaerobic inoc­
ulum sludge which was also originated from the same anaerobic diges­
tion reactor, was replaced the sludge of the previous experiments to 
ensure that the sludge activity stabilized before the next experiment 
started.
2.3. Analysis methods
Total solid (TS), volatile suspended solid (VS), and suspended solid 
(SS) contents were determined by the weighing method [24]. Samples 
were dried at 105 ◦C to constant weight using a DHG-9075 A drying 
oven (Yiheng, China), followed by ignition at 550 ◦C in a KSL-1100×
muffle furnace (Hefei kejing, China). ORP, DO, and pH were measured 
using Mettler-Toledo electrodes, including an InLab Redox Pro ORP 
electrode (Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland), an InLab OptiOx optical DO 
sensor (Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland), and an InLab Expert Pro pH 
electrode (Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland). The COD measured in this 
study was primarily the TCOD (total chemical oxygen demand) of swine 
wastewater. Analyses were performed using the potassium dichromate 
digestion method with instruments manufactured by LH-A230 (Lianhua 
Technology, China). Gas samples (approximately 5 mL) were collected 
from the anaerobic digestion reactors to determine the biogas compo­
sition by gas chromatography (model SP–2100 A, TCD detection, Beijing 
Beifen Ruili Analytical Instrument Co., Ltd.) with He as the carrier gas, 
and the temperatures of the column, oven, and temperature detector 
were 60 ◦C, 90 ◦C, and 105 ◦C, respectively. The methane production 
was determined by multiplying the volume of biogas by the methane 
content in the biogas at hourly intervals.
2.4. Model fitting
The experimental data from all reactors were evaluated for model 
fitting using OriginPro 2021 (OriginLab Corporation, USA), and the 
correlation coefficients (R2) were calculated accordingly. For kinetic 
derivation and subsequent analysis, MATLAB R2022b (MathWorks, 
USA) was employed to construct the mathematical model, generate 
surface plots incorporating the experimental datasets, and perform sta­
tistical parameter fitting.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Kinetics of ORP variation in air mixing–anaerobic digestion
3.1.1. Response of the ORP to DO variation
OPR and DO electrodes are monitoring devices widely used in 
wastewater treatment. DO diffuses rapidly in liquor and is immediately 
consumed by microorganisms and reducing compounds. As a result, the 
oxygen concentration at the electrode surface changes instantaneously. 
This makes it difficult for electrochemical sensors to obtain stable sig­
nals at very low concentrations, resulting in a relatively high detection 
limit for DO electrodes. Because ORP responds sensitively and mono­
tonically to oxygen intrusion, while DO is rapidly depleted and difficult 
to measure at low levels [25,26]. Therefore, ORP can effectively replace 
DO as a more stable indicator of micro‑oxygen conditions [27].
The changes in the DO and ORP in the mixed liquid were measured in 
air mixing–anaerobic digestion (Fig. 1a). When mixing began, the 
changes in the DO and ORP in the mixed liquid exhibited similar trends. 
Both the ORP and DO increased rapidly and then gradually stabilized. 
Origin software was used to determine the quantitative relationship 
between DO and ORP by fitting the data to an exponential model (Eq. 
(1)); the response parameters are shown in Table 1. 
ORPs = k*Ln (CDO) + ORP0
(1) 
In this equation, CDO is the DO content of the mixed liquid at a certain 
time (mg/L); ORPs is the ORP value of the mixed liquid at the same time 
(mV); k is the rate of the response of ORP (mV) to the change in Ln (DO) 
variation; and ORP0 is the ORP value at a DO concentration of 1 mg/L.
This model not only provides a simpler method to determine the DO 
content, and practical approach for estimating DO in air mix­
ing–anaerobic digestion, but also enables the inference of low DO con­
centrations from ORP measurements. This capability provides a 
foundation for further elucidating how oxygen dynamics influence 
anaerobic digestion processes.

the ORP were showed in Fig. 1b–c. When air mixing started, the ORP 
increased rapidly due to the increase in the DO content in the mixed 
liquid. The DO content subsequently no longer increased consistently 
because of oxygen consumption by facultative anaerobes. With the 
balance of oxygen dissolution and oxygen consumption, the DO in the 
mixed liquid tended to stabilize. A similar trend was identified in aerobic 
aeration tanks [28]. The oxidation–reduction reaction also gradually 
became constant, and the ORP tended to be stable. Notably, the ORP 
increased to the maximum ORP value (ORPmax) that could be reached in 
the mixed liquid at a given substrate concentration with increasing 
mixing intensity. The ORP change process and the ORPmax reached in air 
mixing were recorded (the range of the ORP value change and the time 
needed are presented in Table S2).
During 120 min of air mixing–anaerobic digestion, the increase in 
the ORP was influenced by both the organic substrate concentration and 
the air mixing intensity. For example, when the substrate concentration 
was 2 g COD/L, ORPmax was −244 mV at a mixing intensity of 33.3 mL 
air/min. However, at a mixing intensity of 66.7 mL air/min, ORPmax 
reached −219 mV. At 100 mL air/min, ORPmax further increased to 
−120 mV. Under the same mixing intensity, higher substrate concen­
trations led to faster oxygen consumption by microbes [13]. Therefore, 
the increase in the organic substrate concentration reduced ORPmax. 
Specifically, when the mixing intensity was 33.3 mL air/min, ORPmax 
was −120 mV at 2 g COD/L, −136 mV at 4 g COD/L, −195 mV at 6 g 
COD/L, and −237 mV at 8 g COD/L. At 10 g COD/L, ORPmax decreased 
to −357.4 mV. The intensity of air mixing and the organic substrate 
concentration exerted combined effects on oxygen dissolution and 
consumption, which consequently changed the maximum DO and ORP 
that the mixed liquid could achieve.
The rate of increase in the ORP (RORP) was calculated, as shown in 
Table S3. Improving the air mixing intensity significantly increased the 
oxygen dissolution rate. Molecular oxygen has a relatively high ORP 
value (+0.86 V) and can rapidly accept electrons [29]. A low air mixing 
intensity (33.3 mL air/min) brought the mixed liquid with 2–4 g COD/L 
into only a micro–oxygen environment (−300 to −150 mV) [12], and 
the RORP was relatively slow (6.08–6.72 mV/min). However, when the 
intensity was increased to 100 mL air/min at 2–4 g COD/L, the mixed 
liquid directly entered the aerobic environment (> −
150 mv, −120 ~ 
−136 mV). The RORP also increased significantly to 15.9–17.1 mV/min. 
The DO at a high concentration consumed electrons, which caused a 
rapid increase in the ORP. In addition, at the same air mixing intensity of 
100 mL air/min, the RORP was only 10.9 mV/min when the organic 
substrate concentration was increased to 10 g COD/L. The RORP 
decreased by a maximum of 36.3% at 10 g COD/L compared with that at 
2 g COD/L. The high organic concentration of the substrate clearly 
resisted the air mixing–anaerobic digestion system enter the aerobic 
environment.
Both RORP and ORPmax was affected by two factors (the organic 
substrate concentration and mixing intensity). The Michaelis–Menten 
reaction model of two substrates in random order is widely used to 
describe the kinetics of anaerobic digestion [30,31]. A kinetic model of 
the increase in ORP (Eq. (2)) and the maximum ORP (ORPmax) (Eq. (3)) 
in air mixing–anaerobic digestion was developed. The experimental 
results (Tables S2–3) were used to fit the equations, and the kinetic 
parameters (Tables 2 and 3) and simulation results (Fig. 2) were 
obtained.

The coefficient of determination R2 indicated that the two models 
could better reflect the effects of the organic substrate concentration and 
air mixing intensity on the increase in ORP. Pm represents the maximum 
rate of RORP (66.0 mV/min) that can be achieved in the absence of 
organic substrate when the air mixing intensity is much greater than the 
half–saturation constant km (258 mL air/min). Moreover, under high­
–intensity air mixing, the methane production rate can be reduced to 
half of Pm as the organic substrate concentration gradually increases to 
reach the half–saturation constant ks (17.1 g/L).
In addition, assuming that there is no influence from air mixing, the 
system should be in a completely anaerobic environment in the kinetic 
model of ORPmax. ORPbk (−370 mV) was calculated using Eq. (3), which 
is consistent with the ORP range of the anaerobic environment in 
anaerobic digestion. Liu et al. [32] concluded that the suitable range for 
methanogens is −350 mV or even lower. The ORPbk (−370 mV) can be 
regarded as the ORP value that corresponds to the anaerobic environ­
ment that was suitable for methane production when swine wastewater 
was used as the substrate in this study. Moreover, even with a relatively 
high organic substrate concentration, air mixing could have caused 
rapid entry into the aerobic environment (> −
150 mV) when the in­
tensity approached the half–saturation constant km (75.5 mL air/min). 
Although hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria were not affected by the 
aerobic environment, the methanogens were significantly inhibited 
[23]. The period in which the ORP was greater than the ORPbk was 
detrimental to methane production.
3.1.3. Kinetics of the decrease in ORP in air mixing–anaerobic digestion
After air mixing stopped, oxygen was gradually consumed by the 
microorganisms. The oxidizing substances in the mixed liquid were 
reduced, and the ORP also gradually decreased. Lim et al. [33] found 
that increasing the substrate concentration improved the rate of oxygen 
consumption by microorganisms. This finally shortened the time 
required for the ORP to return to an anaerobic environment (−300 mV). 
For example, in anaerobic digestion with 2 g COD/L, at a mixing in­
tensity of 100 mL air/min, recovery to the anaerobic environment took 
181 min. However, for the sample with 10 g COD/L, recovery took only 
28 min. The rapid recovery of the ORP demonstrated that the rate of 
oxygen consumption increased. Together, the DO and organic substrate 
concentrations influenced the rate of decrease in the ORP. The rates of 
increase and decrease in the ORP were analysed quantitatively by 
kinetics.

from an aerobic or micro–oxygen environment. By analyzing the time 
required for the ORP to return to an anaerobic environment, the rate of 
decrease in the ORP (UORP) was calculated (Table S3). The results 
revealed a positive correlation between the organic substrate concen­
tration and UORP. Previous studies have shown that a high organic 
substrate concentration promotes an increase in the oxygen consump­
tion rate by microorganisms and generates more reducing substances 
with low electric potentials [34–36]. The UORP was approximately 
0.595–0.993 mV/min at 2 g COD/L, whereas the UORP was 1.43–1.46 
mV/min at 10 g COD/L. At a mixing intensity of 100 mL air/min, the 
rate of decrease in the ORP at substrate of 10 g COD/L was approxi­
mately 1.45–fold of that at 2 g COD/L.
Both substrate metabolism and respiration can be used by microor­
ganisms to produce energy. The level of DO also determines the rate of 
change in UORP. As a correlation exists between the DO content and the 
ORP in anaerobic digestion (Eq. (1)), the DO value used in this study 
refers specifically to the initial DO concentration at the onset of ORP 
decrease. This initial DO content was calculated from the maximum ORP 
(ORPmax) reached at the end of air mixing (Table S2). The above results 
can be explained by a kinetic model developed as in Eq. (3). The model 
reflects the simultaneous influence of two substrates (organic substrate 
concentration and DO content) on the rate of DO consumption (ORP 
decrease) by microorganisms. The experimental data were fitted to Eq. 
(4) to obtain the kinetic parameters (Table 4, Fig. 3a) for the decrease in 
ORP.

In this kinetic model, Um indicates the maximum ORP decrease rate 
(3.03 mV/min), which can be achieved with a high organic substrate 
concentration and a high DO content. By this calculation, anaerobic 
digestion was estimated to be able to move from a micro–oxygen envi­
ronment to an anaerobic environment (from −150 to −300 mV) in 
approximately 50 min. Furthermore, kS (5.52 g COD/L) and kI (0.056 
mg/L) were able to reflect the extent of the effect of these substrates on 
UORP. The organic substrate concentration and DO content both have 
pronounced effects on UORP. The oxygen consumption rate during the 
decrease in the ORP is correlated with the abundance and activity of 
microorganisms. High DO induces anaerobic microorganisms to in­
crease the expression of functional genes in response to oxidative stress 
[37]. Some anaerobic microorganisms even use the same mechanism to 
consume oxygen [38], which mitigates the damaging effect on anaerobic 
microorganisms. Moreover, a high organic substrate concentration 
provides sufficient nutrients for bacteria to ensure normal growth, 
which is conducive to accelerating facultative anaerobic respiration and 
increasing the rate of oxygen consumption.
3.2. Kinetics of methane production in air mixing–anaerobic digestion
The CH4 content (Fig. 4a–c) and biogas output (Fig. S1a–d) were 
recorded, which were used to estimate the methane output (Fig. 4e–h) 
and methane production rate (Table S4). The results revealed that the 
methane production process can be divided into three phases (abnormal, 
promotion, and normal) (Fig. 4d). The methane production rates in the 
three stages can be designated as Ri, Re, and Rck. In the abnormal phase, 
the methane concentration in the biogas is lower than that in the control 
(no air mixing). The times of abnormal phase includes the air mixing 
time and the recovery time. In the promotion phase, the methane pro­
duction rate increased due to the enhanced mass transfer efficiency and 
the creation of a micro–oxygen environment by air mixing. After the 
mixing effect is mitigated, methane production enters the third phase, 
namely, the normal phase. At this phase, the ORP returned to a reducing 
environment, the DO was completely consumed by microorganisms, and 
the rate of methane production was the same as that of the control.
3.2.1. Methane production in abnormal phase with oxygen inhibition
The CH4 concentrations were extremely low (less than 1%) during air 
mixing. After the air mixing stopped, the CH4 concentration gradually 
recovered to a normal level (more than 40%). However, the methane 
production rate was significantly lower than that of the control under 
the same organic substrate concentration during this abnormal phase. 
For example, at 10 g COD/L, the control reactor exhibited a methane 
production rate of 70.1 mL/h, whereas even at the lowest air mixing 
intensity of 33.3 mL air/min, the rate decreased markedly to 41.1 mL/h, 
which is far lower than that of the control. Meanwhile, organic substrate 
concentration have a substantial impact on the methane production rate 
in the abnormal phase. Under an air mixing intensity of 33.3 mL air/ 
min, the methane production rate was 7.10 mL/h at a COD concentra­
tion of 2 g/L. When the COD concentration increased to 10 g/L, the 
methane production rate rose to 41.1 mL/h, representing approximately 
a 4.79-fold increase. Similarly, at an air mixing intensity of 100 mL/min, 
the methane production rate at 10 g COD/L (37.1 mL/h) was approxi­
mately 10.8 times greater of than that at 2 g COD/L (3.15 mL/h). The 
methane production rate increases with increasing organic substrate 
concentration in the micro–oxygen environment of anaerobic digestion

substrate concentration S (g COD/L), kI is the half–inhibition constant 
based on the DO concentration I (mg/L), and Rck is the methane pro­
duction rate in the control when I is 0 mg/L.
When the DO concentration reached kI (0.132 mg/L), the methane 
production rate was reduced to 50% of the maximum methane pro­
duction rate (Rim, 152 mL/h) because of the inhibition of DO. The kI 
value can also somewhat reflect the degree of sensitivity of the metha­
nogens to oxygen. The lower kI is, the more intense the response of 
methanogens to DO. Trace amounts of oxygen are then able to lead to an 
increase in ORP, thereby significantly inhibiting the activity of the 
methanogens and decreasing the rate of methane production [40]. When 
the DO content is much greater than kI, the methane production rate is 
completely controlled by DO. Seuntjens et al. [41] found that methane 
production is easily and strongly inhibited by DO, and increasing 
methane production requires a higher organic substrate concentration. 
As the organic substrate concentration approaches kS (16.2 g COD/L), 
the methane production rate can reach 50% of the maximum methane 
production rate. When the substrate concentration is much greater than 
kS and the DO concentration approaches 0 mg/L, the methane produc­
tion rate approaches the maximum methane production rate. Thus, this 
competitive inhibition kinetic model can be used to understand the ef­
fects of the organic substrate and DO (mixing intensity) on the methane 
production rate. In addition, in the control (no air mixing), the DO 
concentration was 0 mg/L. At that time, the methane production rate Rck 
was related only to the organic substrate concentration.
3.2.2. Methane production in promotion phase
After air mixing stopped, the methanogens gradually recovered 
normal activity [42] the methane concentration recovered, and entered 
the promotion phase of methane production. The results revealed that 
low–intensity air mixing and high organic substrate concentrations 
could increase the methane production rate (Table S4). Specifically, at 
10 g COD/L, the methane production rate increased to 97.9 mL/h at 
33.3 mL air/min, which was significantly higher than that of the control 
(70.1 mL/h). A micro–oxygen environment can promote hydrolysis and 
mitigate acid accumulation, thereby resulting in an increased rate of 
methane production [43]. Notably, the results revealed that the process 
of promoting the methane production rate lasted approximately 5 h 
(promotion phase), as Fig. 4d showed. The rate of methane production 
subsequently decreased to the level of the control (normal phase). This 
phenomenon has been similarly observed in previous studies [10]. In the 
promotion phase, DO is consumed by facultative anaerobes. The 
methane production rate gradually increased. The methane production 
rate was related only to the substrate concentration. The model can be 
simplified from Eq. (5) to Eq. (6).

Furthermore, Eq. (10) was used to generate Fig. 6, which reflects the 
effects of mixing time and frequency on methane output at 3 mixing 
intensities and 3 substrate concentrations. Under an organic substrate 
concentration of 5 g COD/L and a mixing time of 1 min, when the air 
mixing intensity was 33 mL air/min, air mixing with a frequency of 4 
times/day resulted in a maximum methane output of 984 mL, which was 
13.6% higher than that of the control (no air mixing, 866 mL/d). Under 
the same conditions, when the air mixing intensity was increased to 66.7 
and 100 mL/min, the highest methane output reached 1016 and 1022 
mL/d (a frequency of 3 times/d), which represented increases of 17.4 
and 18.0%, respectively, compared with that of the control. Under the 
substrate concentration of 5 g COD/L, a mixing intensity of 100 mL air/ 
min, and a mixing time of 1 min, methane output at a frequency of 4 
times/d resulted in the maximum value (1022 mL). Under the same 
substrate concentration and air mixing intensity, the methane output 
decreased with increasing mixing time. As the mixing frequency 
increased, the methane output first increased and then decreased.
Under an air mixing intensity of 66.7 mL air/L and an organic sub­
strate concentration of 2 g COD/L, increase of the air mixing time and 
frequency both resulted in a decrease in methane output. When the 
organic substrate concentration was increased to 6 and 10 g COD/L, an 
increase in the mixing frequency increased the methane output. At a 
organic substrate concentration of 6 g COD/L, mixing for 1 min and 4 
times/d resulted in a maximum methane output of 1149 mL/d. When 
the organic substrate concentration was 10 g COD/L, the methane 
output reached a maximum of 1785 mL/d at mixing time of 1 min and a 
frequency 4 times/d. The model further indicates that increasing the 
organic substrate concentration can offset the negative effects result 
from increase of mixing frequency, ultimately leading to an effective 
enhancement in methane output.
Prolonged air mixing time caused the ORP variation and even the 
irreversible damage to the methanogens, which were the major reasons 
for the decrease in output [10]. However, increasing the substrate 
concentration improved the stability of the system significantly. 
Increasing mixing frequency consistently improves mass transfer effi­
ciency. However, the resulting methane output still depends on sub­
strate concentration and mixing time.
3.5. Implication
Although air mixing can significantly enhance methane output, 
excessive mixing time or overly frequent mixing may negatively affect 
anaerobic digestion performance. Therefore, identifying appropriate 
air-mixing parameters is essential for improving process efficiency in 
full-scale anaerobic digestion systems. However, experimentally deter­
mining the optimal combination of organic substrate concentration,

enable prediction of methane output under different organic substrate 
concentrations and air mixing parameters, thereby allowing direct 
optimization of mixing intensity, time, and frequency for full-scale en­
gineering applications. The methane output model and the optimized 
mixing parameters obtained in this study can also be scaled up to full- 
scale biogas plants. For example, in a biogas plant using the swine 
wastewater with an organic substrate concentration of 6 g COD/L as 
feedstock, the optimized mixing parameters can be obtained as follows: 
air mixing intensity of 0.0166 m3/(m3⋅min), mixing time of 1 min, and 
mixing frequency of 4 times per day. Under this condition, the volu­
metric methane production rate in the digester with air mixing can reach 
0.287 m3/(m3⋅d) as agaist 0.248 m3/(m3⋅d) in in the digester with no 
mixing. For the digester with air mixing, each cubic metre of reactor 
volume thus generated an additional 0.035 m3 of methane per day. 
Based on a methane calorific value of 35.9 MJ/m3, this corresponds to 
an energy gain of approximately 1.25 MJ/(m3⋅d). For such air mixing 
intensity, the specific power demand of 26.7 W/m3 (comparable to 
conventional mixing practice [44]) multiply by a total daily mixing time 
of 4 min, resulting in the electrical energy input of about 6.40 kJ/(m3⋅d). 
The energy output still exceeds the energy input with a output-input 
ratio of roughly 195, indicating that the energy consumption of air 
mixing is negligible compared with the additional methane energy 
recovered. These facts indicate that air mixing has a remarkable ener­
getic advantage.
Overall, the development of these kinetic models provides a quan­
titative basis for refining and optimizing air mixing–anaerobic digestion 
technologies, supports the design and operation of full scale biogas 
plants, and offers new insights into methane emission behavior under 
micro oxic/anaerobic alternating environment.
4. Conclusions
This study developed kinetics models quantitatively describing ORP 
variations and methane production, which revealed that high organic 
substrate concentrations fundamentally enhance the resistance of air 
mixing–anaerobic digestion systems to oxygen stress. Elevated substrate 
availability accelerates oxygen consumption and promotes rapid resto­
ration of anaerobic environment, thereby shortening oxygen inhibited 
periods and stabilizing methanogenic activity after air-mixing. The ki­
netic models developed demonstrate that the decrease in ORP showed a 
positive correlation with both the organic substrate concentration and 
the maximum ORP reached at the end of air mixing. The maximum ORP 
increase and decrease rates reached 66.0 and 3.03 mV/min, respec­
tively. Methane production followed abnormal, promotion, and normal 
phases, with a maximum promotion phase rate of 358 mL/h under 
sufficient substrate availability. The methane output model predicted 
daily methane production with errors generally below 15%.
Compared with complex models such as ADM1, the proposed ORP 
based kinetic approach provides a simpler and more practical model for 
analyzing oxygen stress and optimizing air-mixing–anaerobic digestion 
systems. The results provide direct guidance for biogas plant design and 
operation applying the process of air mixing–anaerobic digestion. Given 
the substrate concentration, the mixing parameters can be determined 
according to the developed models. This work demonstrates that limited 
oxygen exposure can be quantitatively managed rather than avoided, 
offering new insights for the design and control of anaerobic digestion 
systems.
